title: Threaded prefetch savings scan - lab memo
content:
Purpose:
Quick lab-run to quantify how adding lightweight "threaded prefetch" workers (slot-local prefetch threads that hydrate KV/prefix cache asynchronously) impacts latency tail and $/token under microburst-dominated session mixes. This is a working notebook for console/tooling folks + serving runtime to discuss feasibility of enabling a low-cost prefetch mode for customer-facing fastpaths.

High-level finding (TL;DR):
- Threaded prefetch reduces p99 latency for small microbursts (~10–30 concurrent short sessions) by ~15–30% depending on model and KV-hit distribution.
- It increases sustained throughput modestly (2–6%) for steady loads with mixed session lengths.
- Cost impact is mixed: additional CPU threads add ~0.8–1.6% infra cost for our config, but token-level cost per response drops when p99 improvements avoid expensive fallback-tier replicas. For bursty workloads the net dollars/10k tokens improved by ~4–9% in our runs.

Experimental setup (what we ran):
- Date: 2029-06-03 to 2029-06-09 (iterative tweaks).
- Hardware: G5x2 machines for core backends (NVIDIA equivalent), 64 vCPU control plane nodes for prefetch workers, 256GB RAM.
- Models: open-llama-13B-v2 (quantized), and bloom-7b-instruct (fp16) as representative shapes (13B dense-ish vs 7B sparse-ish).
- Workload profile: synthetic session mix derived from product telemetry: 70% short (10–40 tokens reply), 20% medium (150–300 tokens), 10% long (500+). Injected microbursts: windows with 10–30 concurrent short sessions for 30–90s.
- Baselines tested: 1) No prefetch (current mainline) 2) Threaded-prefetch enabled (2 prefetch threads per slot) 3) Prefetch + conservative batching (prefetch warms and then grouping of immediate requests).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p99 latency, cold-start penalty (first-turn latency), KV cache hit-rate, CPU consumption on control-plane prefetch nodes, effective tokens/sec, and a simple cost model mapping CPU+GPU minutes to $/10k tokens.

Measurement methodology notes:
- Each experiment was 10 minutes steady-state + 5-minute warmup + 5-minute cool-down, repeated 5 times to get variance.
- Microburst windows aligned across experiments to ensure comparable contention.
- P99 measured using service-observed end-to-end (ingest -> model decode final token).
- Cost model: used reserved instance hourly rates (internal pricing tier), CPU minutes priced per our infra catalog, and included fallback replicas cost when p99 exceeded target (we assume fallback to higher-tier GPU at 30% price premium for impacted requests).

Raw summary (median across runs):
- open-llama-13B-v2:
  - Baseline (no prefetch): p50=42ms, p90=110ms, p99=490ms, KV-hit=0.62, tokens/sec=4200, infra-additional-cpu=0%, $/10k tokens (baseline)= $1.00
  - Threaded-prefetch (2 threads/slot): p50=40ms, p90=95ms, p99=360ms, KV-hit=0.78, tokens/sec=4350, infra-cpu+1.1%, $/10k tokens= $0.93
  - Prefetch+batching: p50=41ms, p90=92ms, p99=345ms, KV-hit=0.80, tokens/sec=4480, infra-cpu+1.6%, $/10k tokens= $0.90

- bloom-7b-instruct:
  - Baseline: p50=36ms, p90=92ms, p99=320ms, KV-hit=0.54, tokens/sec=6800, infra-additional-cpu=0%, $/10k tokens= $0.78
  - Threaded-prefetch: p50=34ms, p90=80ms, p99=250ms, KV-hit=0.70, tokens/sec=7000, infra-cpu+0.9%, $/10k tokens= $0.75
  - Prefetch+batching: p50=35ms, p90=78ms, p99=235ms, KV-hit=0.72, tokens/sec=7120, infra-cpu+1.4%, $/10k tokens= $0.73

ASCII latency shape (open-llama-13B-v2, p99 focus) - median run:
  p99 latency (ms) over time windows (30s bins):
  [baseline]  |████████████████████████████████████████████████| 490
  [prefetch]|███████████████████████████████████             | 360
  [batching] |████████████████████████████████               | 345

Interpretation and patterns observed:
- KV hit-rate correlated very strongly with p99 improvement. Prefetch moves many short sessions from miss->warm state so tail drops.
- The biggest win occurs in microburst ramp-up windows (first 10–30s). If session reuse is high across short bursts, prefetch yields >20% p99 drop.
- CPU overhead is low because the prefetch threads operate opportunistically: they back off on sustained slots and are bounded by a simple token budget per slot (configurable).
- For long-token sessions the delta is negligible; batching optimization yields small extra throughput wins by improving packing efficiency.
- In some pathological adversarial mixes (many short sessions with randomized prompts that defeat prefix locality) prefetch increases CPU without meaningful hit-rate improvement — avoid enabling globally without guardrails.

Cost calculus notes (rough):
- In moderate-burst customers, avoiding fallback replicas (triggered by p99 blowouts) is the dominant savings vector. A 20–30% p99 improvement avoided ~12% of requests hitting fallback tier in our sim, giving net savings despite CPU uplift.
- For very steady high-throughput customers, the CPU overhead translates to higher costs with marginal latency benefit; consider per-customer opt-in or adaptive enabling.

Config knobs we experimented with:
- threads_per_slot: 0 | 1 | 2 | 4 (2 gave best tradeoff in our runs)
- token_budget_per_prefetch: 32 | 64 | 128 (64 balanced hit-rate vs wasted prefetch)
- backoff_ms: 10 | 50 | 200 (short backoff best for microbursts)
- locality_threshold: fraction of identical prefix hits in recent window (used to gate aggressive prefetch)

Open questions / risks:
- Security/privilege: prefetch workers will access KV contents; ensure KMS token scoping and audit logs are enabled for prefetch actors.
- Observability: need per-slot prefetch telemetry (prefetch attempts, bytes read, hit/miss) surfaced in Console with sample traces to tune safely.
- Adversarial workloads: add rate-limiting and optional per-customer opt-out to mitigate wasted CPU.
- Model-generalization: tests touched only two model families; need wider sweep across more architectures (sparsity, longer-context models).

Next recommended steps (practical roadmap):
1) Ship a controlled feature flag gated behind customer tier + opt-in plus default OFF for enterprise until telemetry in place. Owner: Kai Chen. Target: 6 weeks.
2) Add prefetch telemetry to Console (prefetch_attempt, prefetch_success, prefetch_bytes, cpu_ms). Owner: console team. Target: 3 weeks.
3) Run extended sweep across 6 representative models and 3 real-customer anonymized traces. Owner: Miguel Torres + SRE. Target: 4 weeks.
4) Draft rollout playbook: when to enable per-customer, knob defaults, fallback detection. Owner: product-console. Target: 2 weeks after above.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally light on formal statistical tests; we focused on signal discovery. If reviewers want, I can attach raw CSV runs for full ANOVA.
- Consider tying prefetch mode to tiered SLOs (e.g., enable for teams with p99 targets < 400ms).
